note: Non-AI formative self-review for SBA steps. Not official marks.

steps.title: Theme Exploration

checklist.text: My theme comes from my own experience or concern, not a copied online topic.
I listed 3–5 topics I truly care about, each with one sentence on why it matters to me.
I have a mind map that branches into objects, places, people, emotions and social issues.
The four pieces show a clear progression (e.g. personal → interpersonal → social/cultural → reflection/way forward).
I have at least 3 primary images (my own photos or sketches).
I listed 1–3 possible reference artists and the media I want to try.
The theme is feasible in time and materials; I have discussed or will discuss it with my teacher.

guidingQuestions: Which real experience does this theme connect to most strongly?
If the theme is too broad, how can I narrow it to a personal angle?
How will each next piece respond to the previous one?
Which primary photos or sketches can support this theme?
Would a viewer understand what I care about from my keywords alone?
Does the medium I want to try match the feeling I need to express?
sentenceFrames: I chose this theme because I once＿＿, which made me feel＿＿.
Piece 1 will express my own＿＿; Piece 2 will extend to my relationship with＿＿.
My keywords include＿＿,＿＿ and＿＿, all linked to my experience of＿＿.
The four-part arc is: personal＿＿ → interpersonal＿＿ → social/cultural＿＿ → reflection/way forward＿＿.
steps.tip: A theme does not need to sound grand—it needs to be real and developable into four pieces.

redFlagReminders.text: Avoid stiff, curator-style theme blurbs; write in your own voice about experience and feeling.
Do not leave the theme as a slogan—link it to concrete visual elements you will use later.
Do not rely only on online images; keep primary photos or drawings of your own.

steps.title: Reference Research

checklist.text: I have primary research (photos, sketches, survey or interview) and secondary sources, all cited.
I chose at least two reference artists, preferably from different cultures.
Each artist has a Feldman four-stage analysis with visual evidence in the judgement.
Each artist has a “try by myself” practice photo.
I wrote what I learnt and what I chose to reject, and why.
The research connects to my own making—it is not a copied biography.
All images and texts have a complete source list.

guidingQuestions: Which technique from this artist can I transform for my theme?
What surface style did I reject, and why does it not fit me?
How did primary research change my original idea?
After a cross-cultural comparison, how do the two artists express the same feeling differently?
Does my judgement point to concrete evidence in the image?
If I only copy the surface look, how will viewers see through that?
sentenceFrames: From＿＿ I learnt＿＿, which I can use to express＿＿ in my theme.
＿＿ does not suit my work because＿＿.
I think the work expresses＿＿ because＿＿ (visual evidence).
I will borrow＿＿’s＿＿ approach, not imitate the whole style.
Primary research showed＿＿, which led me to add＿＿ in the image.
steps.tip: Research means transform, not cut-and-paste: for every artist, write what you learnt and what you rejected.

redFlagReminders.text: Long passages that sound like the web or AI are a red flag—use your voice and cite sources.
Do not only paste artwork images; link every claim to form and theme.
“Try by myself” needs real practice evidence—not empty words added later.

steps.title: Idea Development

checklist.text: I have a concept map linking keywords, primary material and artist approaches.
I have at least three genuinely different composition options (viewpoint, scale, subject or medium changed).
Each option has strengths and weaknesses written down.
Rejected options are marked × with clear reasons.
My final choice is justified in terms of theme communication and visual focus.
The sketches show the influence of Step 2 research.
I kept rejected sketches; the development trail is complete.

guidingQuestions: What should viewers see first?
Which object or symbol best represents my theme?
What feeling do I want, and which colour, line or texture can create it?
What did I borrow from a reference artist, and how did I make it mine?
Would a different viewpoint, scale or medium work better?
Are my rejection reasons about visual effect and theme—not just “looks bad”?
sentenceFrames: Strength:＿＿; weakness:＿＿.
× Option＿＿: because＿＿ (e.g. too cluttered, theme unclear).
I chose option＿＿ because it expresses＿＿ through＿＿.
This option borrows＿＿’s＿＿ approach, but I changed it to＿＿.
If I enlarge the subject / change the viewpoint, the focus becomes＿＿.
steps.tip: Rejected sketches are evidence of exploration—mark × with reasons; do not delete them.

redFlagReminders.text: Sketches identical to the final piece look like after-the-fact padding—an empty-process red flag.
Only one option with no comparison means little real exploration.
Sketches must show how visual elements carry the theme; do not disconnect from research.

steps.title: Media Experiments

checklist.text: Each piece has at least three material/technique tests.
Each test changes only one variable (material, ratio, tool, surface, etc.).
Each test has a photo or sample labelled with materials used.
There is at least one failed or weak test with reasons written.
I wrote what I will change next, then tested again.
Test questions link to the theme (e.g. which effect best expresses＿＿).
I concluded which approach I chose and how it helps the theme.
Final materials match what appears in the experiment record.

guidingQuestions: Which visual problem is this test trying to solve?
Which variable did I change, and how did the result change?
What did the failed test teach me, and what will I change next?
Which effect best expresses the emotion or idea in my theme?
Am I only asking “which looks nicer” instead of “which fits the theme”?
If every test succeeded once, did I really explore?
sentenceFrames: This test aims to solve:＿＿. I changed＿＿.
The result was＿＿; it looks＿＿. It worked/failed because＿＿.
Next time I will try＿＿ to see if I can＿＿.
This effect can express＿＿ in my theme.
After comparing＿＿ approaches, I chose＿＿ because＿＿.
steps.tip: Treat it like a science experiment: change one variable at a time and photograph failures too.

redFlagReminders.text: No failures recorded is a red flag—add at least one contrast test per piece.
Text-only tests with no photos, or tests that look faked later, signal an empty process.
Link tests to the theme: find the approach that best expresses＿＿, not random material play.

steps.title: Making the Artwork

checklist.text: I have start and stage process photos (app minimum 2; more is better).
I recorded problem → reason → solution entries.
Installation/digital/3D/mixed media has structure photos or layer screenshots (aim for 5+).
Final photos are clear; 3D from multiple angles; animation/multimedia includes a storyboard.
My artist statement is in my own voice; each idea maps to a concrete visual element.
The statement mentions reference-artist influence and why I chose this medium.
The piece clearly continues from research, sketches and experiments.
I declared sources and whether I used any AI tools for help.

guidingQuestions: Do process photos prove I made this myself?
What was the biggest making problem, and how did I solve it?
For each theme idea, where is the matching visual element on the surface?
Did I choose this medium because tests showed it fits the theme?
Does my statement sound like me, or like curator jargon?
If process records were removed, would my teacher still trust this is mine?
sentenceFrames: This piece aims to express＿＿, from my experience of＿＿.
I turned＿＿ into＿＿ [visual element] to show＿＿ [theme idea].
I chose＿＿ because tests showed it can＿＿.
I referred to＿＿’s＿＿ approach but changed it to＿＿ to fit my theme.
Problem:＿＿ → reason:＿＿ → solution:＿＿.
steps.tip: For every concept you write, point to one concrete place or element in the image.

redFlagReminders.text: Polished product with empty process is a major red flag—keep structure or layer evidence for 3D/digital work.
Over-polished long sentences unlike your usual voice suggest AI ghostwriting.
Form disconnected from theme: do not only tell a story—explain how size, colour and texture serve the theme.

steps.title: Reflection and Evaluation

checklist.text: I compared the final piece with Step 1 plans: did I reach the original idea?
My reflection is specific, using “at first I wanted… later I found… so I changed…”.
I reflected from several angles: idea, research, media, skill, viewer response.
I self-assessed with one strength and one improvement point, with evidence.
I recorded peer/teacher comments and how I respond.
I wrote a concrete improvement plan for the next piece.
After Piece 4, I summarised overall progress across the four pieces.

guidingQuestions: Where does the final piece differ from my first idea, and what did I change?
What is most successful, and which part of the image proves it?
If I remade it, what one concrete action would I change?
Which peer/teacher comment do I agree or disagree with, and why?
Compared with the last piece, where did I truly improve?
How will the next piece answer this piece’s weaknesses?
sentenceFrames: At first I wanted＿＿; later I found＿＿, so I changed to＿＿.
The most successful part is＿＿ because＿＿.
If I did it again, I would＿＿ because＿＿.
My peer/teacher said＿＿; I agree/disagree because＿＿.
In the next piece I will try＿＿ to express＿＿ in the theme.
steps.tip: Be honest and evidence-based—“I’m happy / I learnt a lot” is too vague.

redFlagReminders.text: Reflection that sounds unlike your usual writing may be read as AI ghostwriting.
Do not only write successes—failures and next-step plans are also learning evidence.
Nearly identical reflections on every piece, or one catch-up reflection at the end, look like an empty process.
